technique: The Four Horsemen and Their Antidotes
source_citation: John Gottman — The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work; Gottman Institute
problem_it_solves: Falling into the four communication patterns that Gottman's research identified as the strongest predictors of relationship dissolution, without recognizing them or knowing what to do instead.
description:
Gottman identified four communication patterns that predict relationship failure with over 90% accuracy. Criticism attacks the person's character rather than the behavior ('You're so selfish' vs 'I was upset that you didn't call'). Contempt — the most destructive horseman — communicates disgust or superiority through mockery, eye-rolling, sarcasm, or name-calling. Defensiveness responds to criticism with counter-attack or victim stance instead of taking any responsibility. Stonewalling is emotional withdrawal — the listener shuts down, stops responding, and goes emotionally absent.

Each horseman has a specific antidote. For criticism: use a gentle startup that focuses on your feelings and the specific situation rather than attacking character. For contempt: build a culture of appreciation — actively express what you value in the other person on a daily basis, not just during conflict. For defensiveness: take even a small portion of responsibility ('You're right that I could have handled that better'). For stonewalling: signal that you need a break and take a genuine physiological self-soothing break of at least 20 minutes before returning — not a punishing withdrawal, but a biological reset.

The value of this framework is not that it tells you to 'be nicer' — it's that it names specific behaviors you can observe in yourself and in real time, so you can interrupt them before they compound.
when_to_use: When the system detects contempt microexpressions (eyeroll, upper lip curl, condescending tone), stonewalling patterns (near-zero responsiveness, flat vocal energy, gaze aversion), or heavy accusatory 'you' statements with character-level generalizations. The system can flag these in both the user's own behavior and in what they report about their partner.
practice_drill: Watch one of your recorded sessions and identify which horseman, if any, appeared. Write the exact words or tone that represented it. Then rewrite that exchange using the antidote: gentle startup for criticism, appreciation practice for contempt, partial responsibility for defensiveness, a self-soothing plan for stonewalling. Practice the rewrite aloud until it sounds natural and not performative.
common_mistakes: Thinking that avoiding criticism means never raising issues — the goal is raising them without character attack. Confusing stonewalling (which feels self-protective) with healthy pausing — legitimate pausing requires communicating that you'll return. Believing contempt is only dramatic name-calling — subtle sarcasm and condescending tone count and are more damaging because they're harder to name.
